_about: State-specific cremation facts that replace sentences repeated across the state cremation pages. Each 'find' must match the start of exactly one element on the page; each statement carries its source in the README source table. Checked 2026-10-29.
nevada: Get the Nevada provider's General Price List

Nevada ranks who may order a cremation in NRS 451.024: a person named in a valid document or notarized affidavit comes first, then the spouse, an adult son or daughter, either parent, an adult brother or sister, a grandparent and a guardian. When several adult children share that rank, a Nevada funeral home or direct cremation facility may insist that a majority of them agree.
A Nevada provider offering direct cremation must

If none of those relatives can be found, NRS 451.024(2) lets any adult who knew the person sign an affidavit stating how long they knew them and accepting legal and financial responsibility, and that person then has no claim against the estate for the cost.
In Nevada you do not have to buy the urn
A Nevada crematory has to accept an urn or box the family bought elsewhere; if a funeral home pushes back, the Nevada Funeral and Cemetery Services Board handles the complaint.
In short, Nevada has no fixed minimum waiting period

Nevada sets no minimum wait (NRS 451.660), so a cremation can follow as soon as the crematory has the signed death certificate and the authorizing agent's written consent. The cremation rules section further down covers the funeral-director question and the board's complaint number.
georgia: Get the Georgia provider's General Price List

Under O.C.G.A. § 31-21-7, the first say over a Georgia cremation belongs to the person's health care agent, then to anyone named in a notarized disposition affidavit, then the surviving spouse, and only after that to the children, parents and siblings.
A Georgia provider offering direct cremation must

Georgia lets fewer than half of the surviving children act when they have made reasonable efforts to notify the others and know of no opposition from more than half of them, which matters in families where some children cannot be reached quickly.
In Georgia you do not have to buy the urn
Georgia families can supply their own urn; the Georgia Board of Funeral Service takes complaints when a home refuses one or tacks on a fee for it.
Because Georgia is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

Georgia is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance list of nine states that restrict family-directed care, so a family can go to a crematory directly after the local registrar issues the disposition permit.
nebraska: In short, Nebraska has no fixed minimum waiting period

Nebraska sets no minimum wait, so the paperwork controls the timing: a crematory may proceed once it has a cremation authorization form signed by the authorizing agent and the completed cremation or transit permit (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 71-1378). The signer warrants every fact on that form and is personally liable for damage caused by false information. The citation, the funeral-director question and the complaint line are in the cremation rules section further down.
Three paths are standard in Nebraska

Nebraska gives the right of disposition first to anyone named in a notarized affidavit, then the surviving spouse, then the majority of the surviving children, then parents and siblings (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 30-2223). A crematory may follow the first person in a class who signs unless another member of that class objects in writing (§ 38-1425). Direct cremation runs about $1,500 here and cremation with a full funeral about $5,300.
arkansas: Get the Arkansas provider's General Price List

The Arkansas Final Disposition Rights Act (Ark. Code § 20-17-102) lets any adult of sound mind sign a declaration choosing cremation and naming who will carry it out; it must be witnessed by two people, and once it is valid no one else's consent is needed.
An Arkansas provider offering direct cremation must

Without a declaration, the order runs from the spouse to the majority of the surviving children, then parents, siblings, grandparents and grandchildren; a person named on a service member's DD Form 93 outranks everyone.
In Arkansas you do not have to buy the urn

An Arkansas crematory must take the urn the family brings, and a preneed cremation contract can already say where the ashes go (17 CAR § 30-212); complaints go to the Arkansas State Board of Embalmers and Funeral Directors.
Because Arkansas is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

Arkansas is missing from the Funeral Consumers Alliance list of nine states that restrict family-directed care, so a family with the permit and the signed authorization can deal with a crematory itself.
florida: Get the Florida provider's General Price List

Every Florida cremation needs a medical examiner approval number first (Fla. Stat. § 406.11(1)(c)), and the county sets the fee for it: $60 per approval in Orange County since October 1, 2025, $75 in Lee County, $35 for Sarasota and Manatee deaths, and nothing in DeSoto County, as each office listed it when checked on October 29, 2026.
A Florida provider offering direct cremation must

Florida's list of who may authorize a cremation starts with the person's own written instructions (or, for a death in military service, the person named on DD Form 93), then the surviving spouse, an adult son or daughter, a parent, an adult brother or sister, an adult grandchild and a grandparent (Fla. Stat. § 497.005(43)); a provider may rely on one person in a class who says no one else in that class objects.
In Florida you do not have to buy the urn
Florida providers cannot force you to buy their urn, and the Division of Funeral, Cemetery and Consumer Services at the Department of Financial Services takes complaints about one that tries.
In short, Florida sets a 48-hour minimum

Florida's clock starts at death: no cremation for 48 hours (Fla. Stat. § 872.03), and before that window closes the funeral home has usually filed the death certificate, requested the medical examiner's approval number and collected the signed authorization. The rules section further down has the statute text and the state complaint line.

Some Florida families settle on cremation but still want a viewing and service first. That route runs about $6,200 here, against $1,800 for direct cremation, because the visitation, a rental casket and the ceremony all come before the 48-hour wait and the medical examiner's approval clear the way. Ask each Florida funeral home to quote the two paths side by side, since the gap between them varies from one provider to the next.
Families in Florida can choose from three main types

Florida families usually pick among three options. Direct cremation, about $1,800, skips the viewing and ceremony entirely. A memorial service after the cremation can be held whenever and wherever suits the family. A full funeral before cremation, about $6,200, keeps the traditional viewing and service.
Before signing, ask the Florida provider

Before you sign with a Florida provider, find out the expected ready date for the ashes, whether they come back by delivery or pickup, and whether a certified death certificate is part of the quoted price.

Where ashes may be scattered in Florida depends on the place, so check before planning a scattering. Many Florida families instead place the urn in a columbarium niche, bury it, or keep a small portion in memorial jewelry.
Florida cremation pricing lives in two tiers
Florida cremation prices cluster at two levels: about $1,800 for direct cremation, which covers transport, the cremation and returning the ashes, and about $6,200 once a ceremony is added.
connecticut: Get the Connecticut provider's General Price List

Before any Connecticut cremation, a medical examiner has to complete a cremation certificate after inquiring into the cause and manner of death, and the estate pays $150 for it; that fee is not charged for anyone under 18 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-323).
A Connecticut provider offering direct cremation must
The town registrar then issues the cremation permit, which costs $5 by statute, and Connecticut bars cremation until 48 hours after death unless the death came from a communicable disease.
In Connecticut you do not have to buy the urn

Connecticut crematories must keep the cremation permit, the signed authorization and the record of who received the ashes for at least three years (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-322), so a family can ask for copies later; urn complaints go to the Department of Public Health.
Three paths are standard in Connecticut

Connecticut families usually pick one of three routes: direct cremation at about $2,400 with no service, cremation followed by a memorial held later wherever the family likes, or a full funeral with viewing before the cremation. Each one can be adjusted to fit the family.
new-york: Get the New York provider's General Price List

New York Public Health Law § 4201 gives control of the remains to a written agent first, then the surviving spouse, then a surviving domestic partner, then adult children, parents and adult siblings, and that person is the one who signs the cremation authorization.
A New York provider offering direct cremation must

Once a New York crematory accepts the body it must make its best effort to cremate within 24 hours, and if it goes past 48 hours it needs good cause, such as confirming identity (19 NYCRR 203.2). Remains known not to have been embalmed must be cremated as soon as possible after acceptance.
In New York you do not have to buy the urn
New York families can bring their own urn; the Division of Cemeteries regulates crematories, and complaints about a funeral home go to the Department of Health's Bureau of Funeral Directing.
Three paths are standard in New York

New York cremation comes in three versions: direct, about $2,600, with no service; cremation first and a memorial later at a place the family picks, priced in between; and a full funeral with viewing before the cremation, about $8,000.
If a New York death falls under

When the medical examiner or coroner takes a New York case, nothing moves until that office releases the body. Crematories also take out pacemakers, implanted defibrillators and some other implants beforehand, and the removal is not always in the quoted price, so ask about it. The next of kin or authorizing agent also signs a cremation authorization form stating that any battery, power cell or radioactive implant has been removed, and immediate family members may be admitted to the crematory as authorized persons (N-PCL § 1517).
kentucky: Get the Kentucky provider's General Price List

Kentucky's order of who can authorize a cremation starts with someone named in a funeral planning declaration, then the surviving spouse, then the adult children acting by majority, then parents (KRS 367.93117).
A Kentucky provider offering direct cremation must

No Kentucky body may be cremated, or transported to be cremated, without a permit from the coroner of the county where the death occurred stating the cause of death (KRS 213.081). The coroner's permit is needed even when the death was expected, so ask the funeral home how quickly the local coroner usually signs.
In Kentucky you do not have to buy the urn
Kentucky funeral homes have to accept an urn bought elsewhere; the Kentucky Board of Embalmers and Funeral Directors handles complaints about one that will not.
Because Kentucky is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

Kentucky is not among the nine states the Funeral Consumers Alliance lists for restricting family-directed care, so once the coroner's permit is issued the family may work with the crematory on its own.
colorado: In Colorado you do not have to buy the urn

Colorado's Disposition of Last Remains Act puts the person's own declaration first, then a personal representative or the person nominated in the will, then a spouse who was not legally separated, then a designated beneficiary, and then a majority of the adult children (C.R.S. § 15-19-106). If someone in a class will not act or cannot be found, the right moves on.
Three paths are standard in Colorado

Colorado families choose between three routes: direct cremation at about $1,800 with no service, cremation followed by a memorial held later at a place the family picks, or a full funeral with viewing before cremation. Any of them can be shaped around what the family wants.
hawaii: In short, Hawaii has no fixed minimum waiting period

Hawaii sets no waiting period, so timing depends on paperwork: the crematory needs the filed death certificate, the health department permit and a signed authorization. The person who signs is set by HRS § 531B-4, which starts with someone the deceased designated in writing, then a spouse or reciprocal beneficiary, then children, parents and siblings. The rules section lower on the page lists the statute and the complaint line.
In Hawaii you do not have to buy the urn

In Hawaii the family can provide its own urn, and the Department of Health licenses mortuaries and crematories and takes complaints. If no relative steps forward, HRS § 531B-4 lets a willing adult act after giving notice and waiting five days.
Choose a flat-rate direct cremation provider

Compare written direct cremation quotes: even the most basic Hawaii cremation runs around $3,000 on this site's estimates, so knowing exactly what each price covers matters more than haggling over it. Ask how long the ashes take to come back and whether the provider can arrange a scattering at sea.
Three paths are standard in Hawaii

A Hawaii cremation can take one of three shapes. Direct cremation, around $3,000, is the cremation alone. A memorial comes after the cremation, at a place the family picks, and is priced between the two ends. A full funeral with viewing before cremation runs about $8,200.
new-mexico: Get the New Mexico provider's General Price List

When a New Mexican leaves no written cremation instructions, NMSA § 24-12A-2 lets the surviving spouse decide, then a majority of the adult children, then the parents, then a majority of the siblings, then the next heir, and finally an adult who knew the person's wishes. A service member's designee on DD Form 93 overrides that order.
A New Mexico provider offering direct cremation must

New Mexico requires a permit before any cremation, and it is the Office of the Medical Investigator that reviews the death and issues it (NMSA § 24-14-23). Because that review applies to every cremation, not only to suspicious deaths, families should expect it even after a peaceful death at home.
In New Mexico you do not have to buy the urn
New Mexico homes must accept a family's own urn; the New Mexico Board of Funeral Services is the place to complain if one refuses.
In short, New Mexico has no fixed minimum waiting period

New Mexico has no waiting period on the clock; what holds a cremation up is the Office of the Medical Investigator's permit and the signed authorization, and both have to be in hand first. The rules section lower on the page gives the statute and the board's phone number.
Because New Mexico is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

The Funeral Consumers Alliance does not count New Mexico among the nine states that restrict family-directed care, so with the permit issued a family can arrange the cremation directly. The crematory itself must be licensed by the Board of Funeral Services (NMSA 61-32-4), keep its cremation records for at least seven years, and send the ashes back to the funeral establishment within 30 days if no other instructions were given (NMSA 61-32-19.1).
New Mexico providers typically offer three tiers

In New Mexico the choice usually comes down to two price points. Direct cremation, about $1,500, means no viewing or service: the body is cremated and the ashes come back to the family. A full funeral home service before cremation costs about $5,200, or $3,700 more. Under board rules, a crematory may also require pacemakers and other implanted devices to be removed first, at the authorizing family's expense (16.64.10.8 NMAC).

At 65%, New Mexico's cremation rate is above the national average. Cost is the plainest reason, with direct cremation about $4,900 cheaper than a traditional funeral here, but families also value setting a memorial date on their own schedule, some weigh environmental concerns, and nationally more than 60% of deaths now end in cremation.
Ask how long the New Mexico crematory
Ask the New Mexico provider how soon after the medical investigator's permit the ashes are usually ready, and whether delivery is included or only pickup.
new-hampshire: Get the New Hampshire provider's General Price List

In New Hampshire a person can name, in a signed writing, who will control their remains; without one, control goes to the next of kin, a majority deciding when several share the same degree, and a probate court settles deadlocks (RSA 290:17, 290:19). A written designation spares a family that vote at a hard moment.
A New Hampshire provider offering direct cremation must

The crematory sends a copy of the medical examiner's cremation certificate to the chief medical examiner with a $60 fee (RSA 325-A:18), a cost that usually reaches the family through the funeral bill. By law that money goes into the state's medico-legal investigative fund (RSA 611-B:28), not to the crematory.
In New Hampshire you do not have to buy the urn
New Hampshire funeral homes must accept an urn from another seller; the Board of Registration of Funeral Directors and Embalmers handles complaints.
In short, New Hampshire sets a 48-hour minimum

New Hampshire holds every cremation for at least 48 hours after death, unless a contagious disease caused it, and the medical examiner must sign a cremation certificate during that time (RSA 325-A:18). The cremation rules section lower down gives the board's phone number and whether a funeral director is required.
Because New Hampshire is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

New Hampshire does not appear on the Funeral Consumers Alliance's list of nine states that restrict family-directed care, so once the permit is issued a family can work with the crematory without hiring a funeral home. Every crematory in the state must hold a license from the Office of Professional Licensure and Certification, and its operator must have finished a training course from the Cremation Association of North America or the maker of the cremation chamber (RSA 325-A:2, 325-A:4).

In New Hampshire the law sets the first part of the timeline: 48 hours must pass and the medical examiner must sign a cremation certificate before any cremation. After that, turnaround depends on the crematory's workload around Manchester and elsewhere, so ask for the current wait as well as the $2,100 direct cremation price.
Three paths are standard in New Hampshire

New Hampshire providers price three kinds of cremation: direct, about $2,100, with nothing but the cremation; cremation and then a memorial on the family's own schedule, which falls between the two; and a full funeral with viewing beforehand, about $6,800.
Ask how long the New Hampshire crematory
Ask the New Hampshire provider how soon after the medical examiner signs the certificate the ashes are usually returned, and whether delivery is in the price or only pickup.
maryland: Get the Maryland provider's General Price List

Maryland's order for who may arrange a cremation starts with the person's own written designation, then the spouse or domestic partner, an adult child, a parent, an adult sibling and an adult grandchild (Md. Code, Health-Gen. § 5-509). Listing the domestic partner next to the spouse matters for couples who never married.
A Maryland provider offering direct cremation must

If no relative can be reached, another willing adult may sign once the attempts to contact the family are documented, which keeps a Maryland cremation from stalling for weeks. A public official responsible for the disposition may also authorize it when no one else can.
In Maryland you do not have to buy the urn
A Maryland family may buy the urn anywhere; the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors handles complaints.
In short, Maryland sets a 12-hour minimum

A Maryland cremation can happen as soon as 12 hours after death (Md. Code, Health-Gen. § 5-503), one of the shorter waits in the country, provided the next of kin has signed a written authorization. No medical examiner sign-off is needed unless that office took the case. The rules section further down has the citation and the board's number.
Because Maryland is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

Maryland is not one of the nine states the Funeral Consumers Alliance flags for restricting family-directed care, which means a family holding the permit can deal with a crematory itself. Even then, it pays to confirm the crematory's permit first; Maryland crematories are permitted by the Office of Cemetery Oversight, or by the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors when a funeral-home licensee owns most of it.

How fast a Maryland cremation finishes depends less on the law than on the crematory: the legal wait is only 12 hours, but busy Baltimore-area crematories and smaller operators can work through very different backlogs. Ask each provider for its current turnaround alongside the $2,200 direct cremation price, since the cheapest quote is not always the quickest. Whoever runs the cremation must be a registered crematory operator: at least 18, certified by a group such as the Cremation Association of North America, and trained on that crematory's own equipment (COMAR 09.34.06.05).
Three paths are standard in Maryland

Maryland families generally weigh three options: direct cremation at about $2,200 with no service; cremation followed by a memorial whenever and wherever the family chooses, priced between the extremes; or a viewing and funeral before cremation at about $7,000.
Ask how long the Maryland crematory
Ask the Maryland provider how many days after the 12-hour wait the ashes are usually ready, and whether the quoted price covers delivery or only pickup.
massachusetts: Get the Massachusetts provider's General Price List

Massachusetts crematories need two documents before they start: the burial permit and a medical examiner's certificate saying the examiner viewed the body, inquired into the cause and manner of death, and sees no need for further examination (M.G.L. c. 114, § 44).
A Massachusetts provider offering direct cremation must

When the death happened outside Massachusetts, that certificate can come from a medical examiner where the death occurred, which matters for families bringing someone home from another state. Cremation also has to wait 48 hours after death unless a contagious or infectious disease caused it (M.G.L. c. 114, § 44).
In Massachusetts you do not have to buy the urn
Families in Massachusetts can bring an urn from anywhere; the Board of Registration in Embalming and Funeral Directing handles complaints.
south-dakota: Get the South Dakota provider's General Price List

Directions a South Dakotan leaves about their own remains override the family order (SDCL 34-26-1); without them, control passes from a designated person to the spouse, then children, parents and siblings (SDCL 34-26-75). The order then moves to grandparents and more distant relatives, so a niece or nephew can sign only when everyone closer has died or cannot be found.
A South Dakota provider offering direct cremation must

If the coroner is investigating, a South Dakota crematory cannot proceed until the coroner gives a written release (SDCL 34-26A-14). Separately, the crematory needs a signed cremation authorization form and the burial permit before it accepts the body, and it may ask for any other paperwork the county requires (SDCL 34-26A-6).
In South Dakota you do not have to buy the urn
In South Dakota the family can supply its own urn; the State Board of Funeral Service takes complaints.
In short, South Dakota sets a 24-hour minimum

South Dakota requires 24 hours between death and cremation (SDCL 34-26A-13.1); the waiver applies only to a virulent communicable disease. During that day the provider gathers the signed authorization and the burial permit. The section on cremation rules further down lists the board's number.
Because South Dakota is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

South Dakota is absent from the Funeral Consumers Alliance's list of nine states limiting family-directed care, so once the permit exists a family may take the arrangements to a crematory on its own. Each crematory needs a license from the State Board of Funeral Service, and the application must name every certified crematory operator working there and show a refrigerated space for bodies awaiting cremation (SDCL 34-26A-4.1).
South Dakota providers typically offer three tiers

South Dakota providers mostly quote two ends of the range: about $1,500 for direct cremation, with the body cremated and the ashes returned and no service, and about $5,200 for a funeral home service followed by cremation, a $3,700 step up.

This site estimates that about 52% of South Dakota families choose cremation, roughly 11 points below NFDA's 63.4% national projection for 2025. Where families do choose it, cost leads: direct cremation runs about $4,900 less than a traditional funeral in South Dakota. The freedom to set a memorial date later, environmental concerns and a national shift past 60% cremation add to it.
Ask how long the South Dakota crematory
Ask the South Dakota provider how many days after the 24-hour wait the ashes are usually ready, and whether the price covers delivery or only pickup.
california: Get the California provider's General Price List

California gives the right to control a cremation first to an agent under a health care power of attorney, then the spouse (a registered domestic partner has the same standing under Family Code § 297.5), a majority of adult children, the parents and a majority of adult siblings, ending with the public administrator (Health & Safety Code § 7100). Where several children or siblings share a rank, the majority decides.
A California provider offering direct cremation must
Each cremation also needs a disposition permit from the local registrar; Orange County charges $12 and issues it the same day, according to its vital records office when checked October 29, 2026.
In California you do not have to buy the urn
California families may bring any urn; the Cemetery and Funeral Bureau takes complaints about a provider that refuses.
Because California is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

California does not appear on the Funeral Consumers Alliance's list of nine states that restrict family-directed care; after the disposition permit is issued, a family can take the arrangements to a crematory without a funeral home.
indiana: In Indiana you do not have to buy the urn

Indiana's priority order (IC 25-15-9-18) puts a funeral planning declaration or a military DD Form 93 first, then a health care power of attorney, then the spouse, a majority of adult children, the parents and a majority of siblings. A coroner's release is needed only when the coroner investigated the death, and it does not replace the family's authorization.
north-dakota: Get the North Dakota provider's General Price List

In North Dakota, an adult's signed and dated written instruction is enough for a crematorium to proceed without anyone else's consent, though it does not force cremation unless a pre-need contract paid for it (N.D.C.C. § 23-06-03). The instruction has to be signed and dated by a competent adult; a wish mentioned aloud to relatives does not carry the same weight.
A North Dakota provider offering direct cremation must

Without such an instruction, the duty of burial falls on the surviving spouse and then the nearest adult kin, and a disposition-transit permit is still required before the cremation. While a coroner's inquest is required, the coroner keeps custody of the body, so the cremation waits for that release.
In North Dakota you do not have to buy the urn
North Dakota families can supply their own urn; the State Board of Funeral Service takes complaints.
Because North Dakota is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance

North Dakota is not one of the nine states the Funeral Consumers Alliance lists for restricting family-directed care, so with the disposition-transit permit in hand a family can work directly with a crematory.
oklahoma: In Oklahoma you do not have to buy the urn

No Oklahoma cremation can go ahead without a permit from the State Medical Examiner, and state law lets the medicolegal board charge $200 to $275 for it (63 O.S. § 948.1). The right to sign the authorization follows 21 O.S. § 1158: the person's own directions, an appointed representative, the spouse, then the adult children.
Because Oklahoma is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance
Oklahoma is not on the Funeral Consumers Alliance list of nine states restricting family-directed care, so after the medical examiner's permit is issued a family may deal with the crematory directly.
funeral-costs-indianapolis.html: Indianapolis prices sit close to the Indiana picture: about $7,590 for a traditional service and roughly $1,760 for direct cremation on this site's estimates. Funeral homes within Marion County can still differ by more than the gap between Indianapolis and other Indiana cities, so two or three written quotes are worth the phone calls.

The Indianapolis figures here are the Indiana state estimates raised by about 10% for metro costs such as funeral-home real estate and staff wages. The metro also has more providers than most of the state, which gives families room to compare. One charge has dropped out locally: since October 29, 2025, the Marion County Coroner's Office has not billed funeral homes for the cremation authorizations it issues for deaths in the county, according to its indy.gov page when checked on October 29, 2026.

About 48% of Indiana deaths end in cremation, and Indianapolis tracks that share. Price explains much of it: roughly $1,760 for direct cremation against $7,590 for a traditional funeral plus $3,520 for a plot. Cremation followed by a memorial service is the most common middle path in the metro.
According to the National Funeral Directors Association, Indianapolis

At about $7,590, a traditional Indianapolis funeral comes in under the $8,300 national figure from the National Funeral Directors Association. The local number still moves with the type of service chosen and with metro costs, and comparing two or three providers usually brings the total down further.
Direct cremation in Indianapolis is the simplest

About $1,760 covers a basic Indianapolis direct cremation: collecting the body, the paperwork and the cremation itself, with no viewing, ceremony or embalming. Indiana law holds the cremation for 48 hours after death unless the city or county health officer waives the wait in writing (IC 23-14-31-36), and for a death in Marion County the coroner's office asks for up to 24 business hours to process a cremation authorization (317-327-4744). Many families then hold a memorial at a church, at home or in a park.
Direct cremation from $1,760 is the most affordable.

At about $1,760, direct cremation is the lowest-cost route in Indianapolis. Direct burial with no service, a memorial-only service and a home funeral where the law allows are the other low-cost choices, and a casket bought outside the funeral home often costs less. Veterans' benefits, Medicaid and crowdfunding can cover part of the bill, and planning ahead keeps surprise charges off it.
